Assalaamu alaikum! Today we begin a special journey: learning tajweed.
Tajweed means making something good and beautiful. When we read the Quran with tajweed, we say every letter the right way.
The angel Jibreel taught the Quran to the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, and he taught it to his companions, letter by letter. We read it the same way today.
Allah tells us: and recite the Quran slowly and beautifully.
In every lesson I will write on this board, show you the rule in the mushaf, and then you will practise and answer some questions. Ready? Let us begin!
Some letters are heavy: we say them with a full, round mouth. There are seven of them.
Here is a way to remember them: khussa daghtin qidh.
When you say a heavy letter, the back of your tongue rises up, and the sound is full and deep.
All the other letters are light: say them with a thin, flat mouth.
Listen to the difference: saad is heavy, seen is light. Taa is heavy, ta is light.
When al comes before a word, sometimes we say the laam, and sometimes we do not.
Moon letters: we say the laam clearly, as in al-qamar, the moon. In the mushaf the laam has a sukoon on it.
Sun letters: the laam goes quiet, and the next letter is doubled, as in ash-shams, the sun. In the mushaf the next letter has a shaddah.
There are fourteen moon letters. They are all in this sentence: ibghi hajjaka wa khaf aqeemah.
The other fourteen are sun letters. Look at the mushaf: sukoon on the laam, moon. Shaddah after it, sun.
Five letters bounce when they have a sukoon. They are qaaf, taa, baa, jeem and daal.
Remember them with: qutbu jad.
In the middle of a word it is a small bounce, as in yaj-alu.
When you stop at the end of an aayah, it is a big bounce, as in al-falaq.
Be careful: it is a little echo, not a new vowel. Do not say qa, qi or qu.
Ghunnah is a sweet humming sound from your nose. Try it: nnnn, and mmmm.
When noon or meem has a shaddah, we hold the humming for two counts.
As in inna, and thumma. Hold your nose gently: if the sound stops, that was the ghunnah!
Count on your fingers as you hum: one, two.
A noon with a sukoon, or tanween, the double vowel at the end of a word, has four rules. Each depends on the letter after it.
Rule one: izhaar, which means clear. Before the six throat letters, say the noon clearly, with no humming.
The six throat letters are hamzah, haa, ain, haa, ghain and khaa.
As in an-amta in al-Fatihah, and min khayr.
In the mushaf, a clear noon has a sukoon on it, and the two marks of the tanween sit one on top of the other.
Rule two: idghaam, which means merging. The noon melts into the next letter, and the two become one.
Its six letters are in the word yarmaloon.
With yaa, noon, meem and waw, we merge with the humming sound, for two counts. Remember them in: yanmoo.
With laam and raa, we merge with no humming at all.
It only happens across two words, as in hudal lil-muttaqeen. In the mushaf, the next letter has a shaddah.
Rule three: iqlaab, which means changing. It has only one letter: baa.
Before baa, the noon or tanween changes into a meem, with the humming sound for two counts.
Look for the little meem the mushaf writes above it.
As in min baadi: we say mim baadi.
Close your lips softly. Do not press them hard.
Rule four: ikhfaa, which means hiding. It is for the fifteen letters left over.
The noon is not clear and not merged: it hides, half-way between, with the humming sound for two counts.
Your tongue gets ready for the next letter while you hum, and does not press for the noon.
As in min sharri, and innaa anzalnaahu.
In the mushaf, the noon has no sukoon, and the two marks of the tanween are written one after the other.
A meem with a sukoon has three rules. Again, the next letter decides.
Before baa: hide the meem, with the humming sound for two counts, lips closed softly. As in tarmeehim bihijaarah.
Before another meem: merge them, with the humming sound for two counts. As in lahum maa.
Before any other letter: say the meem clearly. As in al-hamdu.
Be extra careful before faa and waw: keep the meem clear!
Madd means stretching a sound. Some vowels are stretched for two counts: this is the natural madd.
Alif after a fathah, waw after a dammah, yaa after a kasrah.
As in qaala, yaqoolu, and qeela. Count on your fingers: one, two.
The little letters count too: the small alif, the small waw and the small yaa are stretched for two.
Not too short, not too long: exactly two.
When a stretch letter meets a hamzah, we stretch it longer: four or five counts.
The mushaf shows it with a wavy line above the letter.
In one word, as in as-samaaa-u, it must be long.
Across two words, as in innaaa a-taynaaka, we stretch it too.
Choose four or five, and keep the same length every time.
Assalaamu alaikum, and welcome to the tajweed class.
In the language, tajweed means to improve something, to make it good. In recitation, it means giving every letter its right: where it comes from and its qualities, and what it is due where it stands.
Allah says: and recite the Quran with tarteel. It is reported from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that tarteel is reading the letters well and knowing where to stop.

There are two kinds of mistakes. A clear mistake changes a letter or a vowel, and can change the meaning: this must always be avoided. A hidden mistake breaks a rule of tajweed, such as a ghunnah or a madd left out.
We read the riwayah of Hafs from Aasim, as most of the world does. The lengths I give you follow the way of ash-Shatibiyyah.
For each topic: I explain on the board, we see it in the mushaf with a reciter, you practise, and then I test you.
Every letter has its own place in the mouth or throat where its sound is made. This is its makhraj.
There are five main areas. First, the empty space of the mouth and throat, where the three madd letters come from.
Second, the throat, in three parts. Deepest: hamzah and haa. Middle: ain and haa. Nearest the mouth: ghain and khaa.
Third, the tongue, the largest area: eighteen letters from different parts of it.
Fourth, the two lips: faa, baa, meem and waw.
Fifth, the nose, where the ghunnah of noon and meem comes from.
To find a letter’s place, put a hamzah with a vowel before it and say it with a sukoon: ab, aq, ad. Where your sound stops is its makhraj.
Tafkheem means making a letter heavy, filling the mouth with its sound. Tarqeeq means making it light.
Seven letters are always heavy, because the back of the tongue rises when they are said. They are called the letters of istilaa.
They are heaviest with a fathah followed by an alif, then with a fathah, then a dammah, then a sukoon, and lightest with a kasrah, but they never become light.
Most other letters are always light. Three change: the raa, the laam of the name Allah, and the alif, which follows the letter before it.
The laam of Allah is heavy after a fathah or a dammah, and light after a kasrah: as in qul huwa Allah, and Bismillaah.
The laam of al, the definite article, is read in two ways, depending on the letter after it.
Before fourteen letters, the moon letters, it is said clearly. This is the clear laam, al-qamariyyah, named after the word al-qamar.
Before the other fourteen, the sun letters, it merges into the next letter, which is doubled. This is the laam ash-shamsiyyah, named after ash-shams.
Why? The sun letters are close to the laam in where they are said, so the laam merges into them. The moon letters are far from it, so it stays clear.
The mushaf shows it: a sukoon on the laam for a moon letter, no sukoon and a shaddah on the next letter for a sun letter.
Look at this alif with a small saad on top. It is the joining hamzah, hamzat al-wasl.
When you start reading from it, you say it. When you join it to the word before, it is dropped.
As in Bismillaah: we do not say bismi allah, but Bismillaah, joining straight on.
When you start with it: in al, say it with a fathah. In a verb, with a dammah if the third letter has a dammah, otherwise with a kasrah.
In a few nouns, such as ibn, ism and imraah, start it with a kasrah.
Qalqalah is an echo, a slight bounce, when one of five letters has a sukoon: qaaf, taa, baa, jeem and daal.
These letters hold back the breath and the sound together, so without the bounce they would not be heard.
The small qalqalah is in the middle of a word or at its end when joined, as in yaj-alu.
The great qalqalah is where you stop, as on al-falaq. With a shaddah, as on al-haqq when you stop, it is strongest.
Do not turn the bounce into a vowel, and do not add a hamzah after it.
Ghunnah is a sound from the nose that belongs to the noon and the meem.
When noon or meem has a shaddah, the ghunnah is complete and held for two counts. This is the ghunnah mushaddadah.
A count is about the time it takes to fold or open one finger at an even pace.
You will meet the ghunnah again in the rules of the noon and meem with sukoon.
The noon saakinah is a noon without a vowel. Tanween is a noon saakinah said at the end of a noun but not written as a noon.
They have four rules: izhaar, idghaam, iqlaab and ikhfaa. Which one depends on the letter that follows.
Izhaar means making clear. Before the six throat letters, the noon is said clearly, with no extra ghunnah.
It is called halqi, of the throat. The throat is far from where the noon is said, so they do not mix.
The mushaf shows a sukoon on the noon, and the tanween marks stacked one over the other.
Idghaam is merging a letter with a sukoon into the next letter, so they are said as one doubled letter.
Its letters are six, gathered in yarmaloon.
With ghunnah, before yaa, noon, meem and waw: the letters of yanmoo. Held for two counts.
Without ghunnah, before laam and raa: the merge is complete, and the noon leaves no trace.
Idghaam happens only across two words. In one word, as in dunyaa, the noon is said clearly.
Iqlaab means turning one thing into another. Before baa, the noon saakinah or tanween turns into a meem.
The meem is then hidden with a ghunnah of two counts, the lips closing lightly.
Why? A clear noon before baa is heavy on the tongue, and it cannot merge, as they are far apart. The meem shares the lips with the baa.
The mushaf writes a small meem over the noon, or in place of the second mark of the tanween.
Ikhfaa means hiding. Before fifteen letters, the noon saakinah or tanween is hidden: between clear and merged, with a ghunnah of two counts.
The fifteen are the first letters of the words in this line of Tuhfat al-Atfal.
And its second half.
The tongue does not touch for the noon. It moves towards the next letter while the ghunnah is held.
Before a heavy letter, the ghunnah is heavy; before a light letter, it is light.
The meem saakinah has three rules, named shafawi, of the lips, as the meem comes from the lips.
Before baa: ikhfaa shafawi. The meem is hidden with a ghunnah of two counts.
Before a meem: idghaam shafawi, also called the small idghaam of two alike letters. Ghunnah of two counts.
Before all other letters: izhaar shafawi. The meem is said clearly.
Take most care before waw and faa: the waw shares the lips, and the faa is close, so people wrongly hide the meem.
Madd is lengthening the sound of a madd letter. The natural madd, madd tabeei, is two counts, no more and no less.
The madd letters are alif after a fathah, waw saakinah after a dammah, and yaa saakinah after a kasrah.
It is natural because it has no cause after it: no hamzah and no sukoon. A cause makes it longer, as we will learn.
The small alif and the small waw and yaa after the haa of the pronoun count as natural madd too.
When you stop on a tanween with fathah, it becomes a natural madd of two counts: ahadaa.
When a hamzah comes after a madd letter, the madd is lengthened. The hamzah is the cause.
Madd muttasil, joined: the madd letter and the hamzah in one word. It is obligatory, waajib: four or five counts.
Madd munfasil, separated: the madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next. It is permitted, jaaiz: four or five counts in our way.
Choose one length and keep it the same through your recitation.
A sukoon after a madd letter is the other cause of a long madd.
Madd aarid lis-sukoon: the sukoon comes only because you stop, as on ar-raheem and nastaeen. Two, four or six counts.
When you join instead of stopping, it is a natural madd of two again.
Madd laazim: the sukoon or shaddah is always there, stopping or not. Always six counts, as in ad-daaalleen.
It is also in the letters that open some surahs, as alif laaam meeem.
The raa is sometimes heavy and sometimes light, depending on its vowel.
With a fathah or a dammah it is heavy, as in rabbi and rizqan.
With a kasrah it is light, as in rijaal.
With a sukoon, it follows the vowel before it: heavy after a fathah or dammah, as in maryam; light after a kasrah, as in firawn.
But it is heavy after a kasrah if the kasrah is only for starting, as in irjiee, or if a heavy letter follows in the word, as in mirsaadaa.
Waqf is stopping at the end of a word to take a breath, meaning to carry on.
When you stop, the last vowel becomes a sukoon. A tanween with fathah becomes an alif, and a taa marbootah becomes a haa.
The mushaf guides you. A small meem: stop here, it is necessary. Laa: do not stop.
Jeem: stopping and joining are both fine. Sala: joining is better. Qala: stopping is better.
Three dots in two places: stop at one of them, not at both.
Ibn al-Jazari wrote in his poem on tajweed that taking up tajweed is a firm duty, and that the Quran came down from Allah with it, and reached us that way.
The scholars say: knowing the rules in detail is a communal duty, while reciting with tajweed, free of clear mistakes, is asked of everyone who recites.
Our two main texts are Tuhfat al-Atfal by al-Jamzuri, on the noon and the madd, and the Muqaddimah of Ibn al-Jazari, on the letters and their qualities.
Tajweed is learnt by hearing it from a teacher and reading back to him. This class prepares you, and does not replace a teacher with ijazah.
Ibn al-Jazari counts seventeen points within these five areas. The tongue alone has ten.
Take care with letters near one another: the daad from the side of the tongue against the upper molars, the dhaa from the tip of the tongue with the tips of the upper front teeth.
Four of the seven are also letters of itbaq, where the tongue presses against the roof of the mouth: saad, daad, taa and dhaa. They are the heaviest of all.
Be careful not to make a light letter heavy next to a heavy one, as in the seen of mustaqeem, or the taa of tatahhara.
This rule is for the laam of the definite article only. A laam that is part of the word is always clear, as in iltaqaa and alhaakum, except before a laam or a raa.
The nouns are learnt by listening: ibn, ibnah, imru, imraah, ithnan, ithnatan and ism.
Where the dammah of the third letter is only temporary, start with a kasrah: imshoo, iqdoo, ibnoo.
Do not confuse it with the silent alif after the waw of the plural, as in kafaroo. It is written, and never said.
The five letters share two qualities: jahr, where the breath is held, and shiddah, where the sound is held. The bounce lets them be heard.
Scholars differ on the colour of the bounce: some follow the vowel before, others lean it towards a fathah. Follow your teacher.
The ghunnah is strongest on a doubled noon or meem, then in idghaam, then in ikhfaa, and weakest on a noon or meem with a vowel.
Before a heavy letter, the ghunnah of ikhfaa takes on heaviness too, as in yansurukum.
Al-Jamzuri lists the throat letters in order, from the deepest: hamzah and haa, then ain and haa, then ghain and khaa.
The iz-haar is clearest before the hamzah and haa, the deepest letters, and least before the ghain and khaa.
Into yaa and waw the merge is incomplete: the ghunnah of the noon remains. Into noon and meem it is complete, with the ghunnah of the doubled letter.
Four words keep the noon clear, as the noon and the yaa or waw are in one word: dunyaa, bunyaan, sinwaan and qinwaan.
Hafs also reads yaa seen wal-quran, and noon wal-qalam, with the noon clear.
It is in one word, as in ambiaahum, and across two words, as in min badi.
Most teachers close the lips lightly, without pressing; some leave a slight gap. Follow your teacher.
It is called true ikhfaa, haqeeqi, as the hiding is agreed upon by all the readers.
The hiding is strongest before taa, daal and taa, nearest to the noon, and weakest before qaaf and kaaf, the furthest.
The mushaf shows a sukoon on the meem for izhaar; no sukoon for ikhfaa; and no sukoon with a shaddah on the next meem for idghaam.
In ikhfaa shafawi, most teachers close the lips lightly; some leave a slight gap. Follow your teacher.
A hamzah before the madd letter, as in aamanoo, makes madd al-badal. For Hafs it stays two counts.
A waw or yaa with sukoon after a fathah, before a letter you stop on, is madd al-leen: two, four or six counts, as in khawf.
By the way of Tayyibat an-Nashr, Hafs also reads the separated madd short, two counts. Do not mix the ways in one recitation.
If you stop on a joined madd whose hamzah ends the word, as as-samaa, you may stretch four, five or six.
Madd laazim has four kinds: in a word with a shaddah, as ad-daaalleen; in a word with a plain sukoon, as aaal-aan in Surah Yoonus.
And in the opening letters, with a merge, as the laam of alif laam meem, or without, as saad.
The opening letters read with six are in: kam asal naqas. The ain of kaaf haa yaa ain saad and of ain seen qaaf may be four or six.
When you stop on a raa, look before it: after a kasrah or a yaa saakinah it is light, as in qadeer. Otherwise it follows the vowel before, as in al-fajr, which is heavy.
A few words allow both, such as firq in Surah ash-Shuara, and misr and al-qitr when stopping. Your teacher will show you which to prefer.
Umm Salamah described the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, reciting and pausing at the end of each aayah, as narrated by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.
A stop that spoils the meaning is to be avoided. If you must stop there for breath, go back and start from a place where the meaning is sound.
When two letters meet, the first with a sukoon and the second with a vowel, the first often merges into the second.
Alike, mithlayn: the same letter, always merged, as in idrib bi-asaaka.
Related, mutajaanisayn: the same makhraj but different qualities, as qad tabayyana, athqalat daawaa, yalhath dhaalik, irkab maanaa.
In basatta, the taa merges but its heaviness stays: an incomplete merge.
Close, mutaqaaribayn: letters near in makhraj, as qur rabbi, and nakhlukkum, which is usually merged completely.
A saktah is a short pause, without taking a breath, about two counts.
By the way of ash-Shatibiyyah, Hafs makes it in four places, marked in the mushaf with a small seen.
In al-Kahf: iwajaa, then qayyimaa. And in Yaseen: min marqadinaa, then haadhaa.
In al-Qiyaamah: man, then raaq. And in al-Mutaffifeen: bal, then raan. Here it keeps the noon and the laam from merging into the raa.
